candidates.source_comment_text: The line about accent being identity rather than noise is the one that stayed with me, because it's the first thing a listener hears and usually the first thing a system flattens out. What interests me is what happens after the tech works. I designed and deliver a 6-week AI fundamentals programme for small business owners in Nigeria, and the barrier there is almost never the capability of the model. It's that people are quietly unsure what to do with it, and a fair number start out assuming these tools were built for somebody else. A system that answers in the register you'd use at home removes one layer of that hesitation, but the working knowledge still has to be built, because knowing a tool can speak your language doesn't tell you what to ask it for. On your question, Yoruba and Hausa with Pidgin as the connective tissue, because Pidgin is what carries a conversation when two speakers don't share a first language. It's also the register a small trader would use with a customer, which makes it the combination more likely to get real commercial use rather than admiring demos.
